items.title: Chico Hamilton interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 30, 2000
items.q: Gene Krupa. They’re all — that’s how broad and beautiful this whole thing is in regards to playing or approaching that instrument.

ctx.x: And active I guess. If you can be real honest, and don’t worry about your ego, can you tell me where do you fit in the line of drummers in innovation and in your music? I mean I don’t know if I asked that question very well but—

Well I don’t know. I’m being very honest. First of all it’s totally impossible for two drummers to play alike, because of the physical aspect. One might have long arms, one might have short arms. And if you have short arms that means that you have to sit closer to your instrument. If you have long arms you sit back, that type of thing, for reach. And just the space between makes a difference in the sound you’re going to get, or the touch you’re going to acquire to get the sound. I don’t sound like anybody else,…

It’s usually left to the non-musicians I guess to try to put down, this guy was influenced by this guy, influenced by this guy, and so forth. Sometimes it’s true and sometimes maybe not. © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

items.title: Chico Hamilton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: But Gene Krupa was just the opposite. I mean Gene was dynamite, very nice man. We got along beautifully, you know.

ctx.x: Okay, so let’s go back and look at your involvement with music. You say you picked up the clarinet because your buddy Jack was playing it. What kind of music were you listening to and what kind of music were you playing?

There was only one kind of music at that time, which was dynamite, was swing. Man, I’d wake up every morning going to school listening to Benny Goodman, right, (musical sounds) Don’t Be That Way, and Gene Krupa used to (musical sounds). First of all man, that was the beautiful thing about LA, the educational system. The requirement you had to take some form of music, either it was playing an instrument, whatever, music theory or whatever, listening or whatever. You had to be involved with some kind of music…
So what did you do when you went to meet the band? You would stand on the platform when they came off?
